lead: Electronic fuel control estimates or measures the air entering the engine, computes the fuel mass needed, and holds each injector open for the time that delivers it. An oxygen sensor in the exhaust reports what actually burned, and the controller trims the pulse. Every modern petrol car runs this loop.
prereq: You need: 4.4 for open and closed loop control, and Unit 3 for the MAP (manifold absolute pressure), throttle and oxygen sensors and for stepper and solenoid actuators.

sections.h3: Why the carburettor had to go

blocks.text: A carburettor lets incoming air speed up through a narrow throat called a venturi; the pressure drop there sucks fuel out through a jet. The jet is a fixed hole, so fuel flow follows air flow only as well as the venturi curve allows, and nothing measures the result. On a hot afternoon, on a cold start, or when the throttle snaps open, the mixture drifts away from the ratio the catalyst needs. Emission norms tighten that ratio at every stage (see emission norms and Bharat Stage standards), and a fixed jet cannot follow.

Electronic carburetion was the stop-gap. A solenoid valve bled air into the carburettor's fuel passages, and the controller moved it from the exhaust oxygen signal. It held λ = 1 at steady cruise, but fuel was still atomised by venturi vacuum and cylinder-to-cylinder distribution stayed uneven.
Petrol injection replaced the jet with a solenoid valve per cylinder, opened for a computed time. Three layouts exist.

items: Throttle-body injection (TBI): one or two injectors above the throttle. Cheap, but slow to respond to transients.
Port fuel injection (PFI): one injector per cylinder in the intake port above the valve. The fuel has a whole intake stroke to evaporate. This is the common layout.
Direct injection (GDI): the injector sprays into the cylinder at 100 bar or more. It cools the charge and allows lean stratified running, but it makes fine soot particles.

sections.h3: The injector and the fuel calculation

blocks.text: Inside the injector is a solenoid: a coil, an armature and a needle held on its seat by a spring. Current in the coil pulls the needle up, fuel at rail pressure sprays, and when the current stops the spring closes the valve in about a millisecond.

The static flow rating is the mass of fuel the injector passes per second when held fully open, in g/s or cc/min, always quoted at a stated pressure, usually 3 to 4 bar for port injection. Flow rises roughly as the square root of pressure. Two drive methods are used.

items: Saturated drive: battery voltage is held across the coil for the whole pulse. Simple and cheap; the needle opens slowly, so it suits small injectors.
Peak-and-hold drive: about 4 A for the first millisecond pulls the needle open fast, then the driver drops to about 1 A to hold it. Large injectors need this, and the coil runs cooler.

blocks.text: The controller turns an air mass into a pulse in four steps.

items: Estimate the trapped air mass flow from speed density.
Divide by the air-fuel ratio to get fuel mass flow.
Divide by the number of injections per second to get fuel per injection.
Divide by the injector flow to get the open time.

blocks.where: m_air is air mass flow in kg/s; η_v is volumetric efficiency, the air actually trapped divided by the swept volume's worth, typically 0.8 to 0.9 at full load, and slightly above 1 is possible with tuned intake and exhaust; ρ is intake air density in kg/m³, from the MAP (manifold absolute pressure) sensor and the intake temperature sensor; V_d is total engine displacement in m³; N is engine speed in revolutions per second. The ÷2 is because a four-stroke inducts air only every second revolution.
t_inj is injector open time in s; AFR is the air-fuel ratio by mass, 14.7 for petrol at λ = 1; n_cyl is the number of cylinders; Q_inj is the injector static flow in kg/s.

blocks.text: Many engines measure the air directly with a hot-wire or hot-film air-flow meter (MAF) instead of speed density. The fuel calculation, the trim loop and the fault reasoning stay the same once the air mass flow is known.

sections.h3: Closed loop, fuel trim and the actuators

blocks.text: The narrowband oxygen sensor is a zirconia cell whose voltage switches sharply as the exhaust crosses λ = 1: high when rich, low when lean (see Unit 3). It does not say how rich or how lean. The controller therefore steps the pulse up and down and watches for the switch to reverse. That hunt around λ = 1 is closed loop.

Short-term fuel trim (STFT) is the instant correction, a percentage added to or taken from the base pulse, usually limited to about ±25%. When STFT stays biased, the ECU learns the offset into a long-term fuel trim (LTFT) table, so the next time the engine runs at that speed and load it starts from the corrected value. LTFT hides a dirty air-flow sensor or a clogged injector until it hits its limit and sets a fault code.
Three actuators work alongside the loop.

items: EGR valve: a stepper motor, or a vacuum diaphragm switched by a solenoid, opens a passage from exhaust to intake. It dilutes the charge and lowers peak flame temperature, which cuts NOx.
Idle air stepper motor: a pintle moves in and out to bypass air around the closed throttle. It sets idle speed hot or cold, and lifts it when the alternator or the air-conditioner loads the engine.

EVAP purge solenoid: opens to draw petrol vapour stored in the canister into the intake. That vapour is extra fuel, so the oxygen sensor reads rich and the ECU shortens the injector pulse to keep λ = 1.

figure.caption: Air charge sets a base pulse from the calibration map (look-up table, not the MAP sensor); the injector fires, the exhaust sensor reads lambda, and the correction returns to the base pulse.

spec.title: Closed-loop fuel control
spec.aria: Air charge sets a base pulse from the calibration map, the injector fires for 8.94 ms, the oxygen sensor measures lambda, and the fuel trim feeds a correction back into the base pulse.

examples.question: A four-cylinder 1.6 L petrol engine runs at 3000 rpm with volumetric efficiency 0.85. Intake air density is 1.16 kg/m³ and the air-fuel ratio is 14.7:1. Each injector flows 3.0 g/s when held fully open. Find the air mass flow, the fuel mass flow, the fuel per injection and the injector open time.
steps: Air inducted per revolution = V_d ÷ 2 = 1.6 L ÷ 2 = 0.8 L = 0.0008 m³.
Speed N = 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 rev/s, so swept flow = 0.0008 × 50 = 0.04 m³/s.
Each injector fires 50 ÷ 2 = 25 times a second; four injectors give 100 injections a second.
examples.answer: Air flow 39.44 g/s, fuel flow 2.68 g/s, 26.83 mg per injection, injector open time 8.94 ms.
examples.check:
Vd = 1.6e-3
N = 3000/60
eta_v = 0.85
rho = 1.16
afr = 14.7
Q = 3.0
n_cyl = 4

swept = (Vd/2)*N
air_g = eta_v*swept*rho*1000
fuel_g = air_g/afr
inj_per_s = n_cyl*(N/2)
per_inj_mg = fuel_g/inj_per_s*1000
pulse_ms = (per_inj_mg/1000)/Q*1000

for v in (air_g, fuel_g, per_inj_mg, pulse_ms):
    print(round(v, 2))

traps: Using the full displacement per revolution: a four-stroke inducts air into only half its cylinders per revolution, so divide V_d by 2.
Mixing densities: speed density needs the intake manifold density from MAP and intake temperature, not an ambient bench figure, and η_v must not be dropped.
Confusing milliseconds with milligrams: pulse width is time, fuel per injection is mass; the injector flow converts one to the other.
Thinking the oxygen sensor sets the mixture: it only trims a base pulse that comes from the calibration map, and it is cold and inactive during a cold start.
Swapping the trims: STFT is the instant correction, LTFT is the value learned and stored against speed and load.

quiz.q: State the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of petrol by mass and say what λ = 1 means.
quiz.a: 14.7:1 — 14.7 kg of air for 1 kg of fuel. λ = 1 means the actual air-fuel ratio equals this stoichiometric value.

quiz.q: Why can a carburettor not hold λ = 1 across all speeds and loads?
quiz.a: Its jets are fixed holes, so metering follows the venturi pressure drop, not a measured air mass. Air density, transients and cold running all shift the mixture, and there is no exhaust feedback to correct it.

quiz.q: Distinguish short-term and long-term fuel trim.
quiz.a: STFT is the instant percentage correction applied while the controller hunts around λ = 1. LTFT is the learned offset stored against speed and load and used as the new starting point, adapting for wear, a dirty sensor or low fuel pressure.

quiz.q: An engine takes 30 g/s of air at an air-fuel ratio of 14.7:1. Four injectors each fire 40 times a second and each flows 2.5 g/s when open. Find the injector open time.
quiz.a: Fuel = 30 ÷ 14.7 = 2.041 g/s. Injections per second = 4 × 40 = 160. Fuel per injection = 2.041 ÷ 160 = 12.76 mg. Open time = 0.01276 ÷ 2.5 = 5.1 ms.

quiz.q: Long-term fuel trim reads +18% at idle but only +2% at cruise. What single fault explains this, and why?
quiz.a: Unmetered air leaking in after the air-flow meter or manifold-pressure sensor, such as a split hose, a worn gasket or a leaking brake booster. At idle the metered charge is small, so the same leak is a large fraction of it and needs a large correction; at cruise the metered charge is several times larger, so the leak is a small percentage.

quiz.q: Name the two solenoid injector drive methods and one advantage of each.
quiz.a: Saturated drive: simple, cheap circuit, suits small injectors. Peak-and-hold drive: the needle opens faster and the coil runs cooler, needed for large injectors.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now blend port and direct injection to keep particulates low while still cooling the charge. Gasoline particulate filters, the petrol twin of the diesel filter, are fitted to meet the latest stages. Model-based charge estimation replaces the steady-state speed-density map with a filling-and-emptying model of the intake manifold. Wide-range linear lambda sensors give a measured λ instead of a rich-or-lean decision. Search next: gasoline particulate filter, wide-range lambda sensor, stratified charge GDI.
